posts.title: The color of uniformity: Far-red light effects on plant growth
posts.excerpt: Ever wandered through a field of plants and observed how their heights are relatively uniform? In nature, this is partly due to plants' ability to sense their neighbors through light receptors and shade-avoidance responses. When a lower ratio of red to far-red (FR) light is detected due to the presence of neighboring plants, plants elongate their stems to compete for light.

posts.title: Is camouflage a form of communication?
posts.excerpt: A researcher from Tokyo Metropolitan University has proposed a new interpretation of camouflage in nature. Most theories dismiss it as a form of communication because there is no apparent "signal" but rather a lack of one. Using an information-theoretic approach, the researcher shows that camouflage can be framed as an "information-masking" signal, one that disrupts the flow of information. The same idea might be applied to the wider field of communication, where signals may actively conceal information rather than convey it.

posts.title: Quantifying dark modes to advance polariton chemistry
posts.excerpt: Researchers have resolved a long-standing paradox in polariton chemistry—a field that explores how to control chemical reactions by trapping molecules inside optical cavities where light and matter strongly interact (known as strong coupling). Previously, a major theoretical hurdle stood in the way: Calculations indicated that millions of inactive molecular states—known as dark modes—should greatly outnumber active polaritons, making it seemingly impossible for light-matter coupling to influence chemistry.

posts.title: New mechanical modulation method enables tunable multi-pulse fiber lasers
posts.excerpt: In a study published in Optical Fiber Technology, researchers from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed a new method to control multi-pulse generation in a 1972-nm mode-locked fiber laser. By applying external mechanical modulation to the optical fiber, the researchers generated multiple adjustable pulse patterns without increasing the pump power. This offers a simpler and more flexible approach to controlling ultrafast laser output.

posts.title: Wildfire modeling helps managers decide where to build and maintain fuel breaks
posts.excerpt: Fuel breaks are linear strips of land along which vegetation is cleared or thinned—constructed along ridgelines, roads and other strategic places—to give firefighters a better chance to safely slow or steer a fire. Often described as "speed bumps" for wildfires, fuel breaks rarely stop fire spread on their own, but they do give crews critical anchor points for building firelines, setting backfires or safely applying water and retardant. They have been used since the 1960s across many landscapes.

posts.title: The experiments improving our understanding of volcanic tsunamis
posts.excerpt: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because of the complex dynamics governing how falling rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate waves. Researchers have used laboratory experiments to study this process, but little is known about how well these models mimic reality.

Yet it has shown considerable decline over the last century, with aridification spreading across East Asia.

posts.title: The Areni-1 Cave Shoe in Yerevan, Armenia
posts.excerpt:
This leather shoe was discovered in Areni 1 cave during excavations in 2008. 
 Made from a single piece of cowhide leather, and still with its leather laces it has been measured as corresponding to a modern US size 7 / EU size 37 / UK size 6. It is stuffed with grass to either maintain its shape or keep the foot warm. It is unknown at this stage whether it was a man or woman's shoe. 
 Researchers have managed to date it back to 3600-3500 BC based on the radiocarbon dating.

posts.title: How a warming ocean is changing the base of the marine food web
posts.excerpt: Climate change is causing warming in the oceans, which can have significant effects on marine food webs. Rising ocean temperatures can intensify seawater stratification, a process in which ocean water forms layers of different densities that mix less readily. This can reduce the supply of nutrients to surface waters and favor smaller phytoplankton species that are better adapted to low-nutrient conditions. Phytoplankton support zooplankton, which in turn transfer energy to fish and other animals. Changes in phytoplankton communities can therefore lead to cascading effects on marine food webs.

posts.excerpt: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. posts.title: Nuclear softening at an embryo's two-cell stage may be vital for further embryonic development
posts.excerpt: A research team led by Kyushu University and the National Institute of Genetics has discovered that during the two-cell stage of mouse embryonic development, the embryo's nucleus softens and deforms. This nuclear softening is an integral part of major zygotic gene activation, where approximately 2,000 genes necessary for embryonic development activate simultaneously. This indicates that nuclear softening is a critical step for further embryonic development.

posts.title: Atlas Obscura’s Guide to America’s Most Haunted Cemeteries
posts.excerpt:
It’s nice to imagine death as an endless deep sleep, but not everyone is so lucky. In cemeteries across the U.S., you’ll find souls whose final resting places are not, in fact, restful at all.
